summary.text: For the exponents 3 and 4, the congruence \(10^i\equiv1+9i\) modulo \(27\) or \(81\), applied to a number and its reversal, forces their common digit sum to be divisible by the modulus; within 3 or 9 digits, positivity then forces every digit to be 9 (while the exponent-2 case is immediate), proving the required minima. For \(n=5+p\), starting with the 11-digit palindromic multiple \(29799999792\) of \(3^5\) and repeatedly concatenating three copies adds a factor of 3 and triples the length, producing a palindromic multiple of \(3^{5+p}\) with \(11\cdot3^p<3^{p+3}\) digits and hence smaller than the corresponding all-nines number.

full_proof.text:
Let \(\operatorname{rev}(N)\) denote the integer obtained by reversing the decimal digits of \(N\), with any leading zeros created by the reversal discarded. For a positive integer \(q\), let \(a(q)\) be the least positive multiple \(N=kq\), \(k\geq 1\), such that \(q\mid \operatorname{rev}(N)\), provided such a multiple exists.

We prove that, for every integer \(n\geq 2\),
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n\in\{2,3,4\}.
\]

The proof has two parts. First we determine \(a(9),a(27),a(81)\). Then, for every \(n\geq5\), we construct a much shorter palindromic multiple of \(3^n\), showing that the displayed all-nines number cannot be minimal.

### 1. A decimal-digit rigidity argument

Write the decimal digits of a nonnegative integer \(N\), starting with the units digit, as
\[
N=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1} d_i10^i,
\qquad 0\leq d_i\leq9.
\]
For \(N>0\), the most significant digit \(d_{m-1}\) is nonzero and \(m\) is the number of decimal digits of \(N\). Put
\[
S=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}d_i,
\qquad
W=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}i d_i.
\]

For every \(i\geq0\),
\[
10^i=(1+9)^i\equiv 1+9i\pmod{81},
\]
because every term of degree at least two in the binomial expansion contains a factor \(9^2=81\). The same congruence is therefore valid modulo every divisor of \(81\), in particular modulo \(27\) and modulo \(81\).

Consequently,
\[
N=\sum_i d_i10^i\equiv \sum_i d_i(1+9i)=S+9W\pmod M,
\]
where \(M\) is either \(27\) or \(81\).

The reversed integer has the digit expression
\[
\operatorname{rev}(N)=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}d_i10^{m-1-i}.
\]
This formula remains valid even if \(d_0=0\), since a leading zero in the reversed digit string contributes nothing. Thus
\[
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{rev}(N)
&\equiv \sum_i d_i\bigl(1+9(m-1-i)\bigr)\pmod M\\
&=S+9(m-1)S-9W.
\end{aligned}
\]

Suppose now that both \(N\) and \(\operatorname{rev}(N)\) are divisible by \(M\). Adding the preceding two congruences gives
\[
0\equiv \bigl(S+9W\bigr)+\bigl(S+9(m-1)S-9W\bigr)
=S(9m-7)\pmod M.
\]
But
\[
9m-7\equiv -7\equiv2\pmod3,
\]
so \(9m-7\) is relatively prime to \(3\), and hence relatively prime to both \(27\) and \(81\). It is therefore invertible modulo \(M\). We conclude that
\[
M\mid S.
\]

This has strong consequences when \(N\) has few digits.

#### Rigidity modulo \(27\)

Suppose
\[
0\leq N<10^3,
\qquad 27\mid N,
\qquad 27\mid\operatorname{rev}(N).
\]
If \(N=0\), there is nothing to prove. If \(N>0\), it has at most three digits, so
\[
0<S\leq 9m\leq27.
\]
Since \(27\mid S\), necessarily \(S=27\). Equality throughout the bound \(S\leq9m\leq27\) forces \(m=3\), and all three digits must equal \(9\). Hence
\[
N=999.
\]
Thus every such \(N\) is either \(0\) or \(999\).

#### Rigidity modulo \(81\)

Similarly, suppose
\[
0\leq N<10^9,
\qquad 81\mid N,
\qquad 81\mid\operatorname{rev}(N).
\]
For \(N>0\), there are at most nine digits, and therefore
\[
0<S\leq9m\leq81.
\]
As \(81\mid S\), we must have \(S=81\). This forces \(m=9\) and every digit to be \(9\). Therefore
\[
N=999999999.
\]
Hence every such \(N\) is either \(0\) or \(999999999\).

### 2. The three exceptional values

We now compute the sequence at \(9,27,81\).

First, \(9\) is itself a palindrome and is divisible by \(9\). Thus it is an admissible positive multiple of \(9\). Every positive multiplier is at least \(1\), so no positive multiple of \(9\) can be smaller than \(9\). Hence
\[
a(9)=9.
\]
Since
\[
10^{3^{2-2}}-1=10^1-1=9,
\]
the required equality holds for \(n=2\).

Next,
\[
999=37\cdot27,
\]
and \(999\) is a palindrome. Thus \(999\) is admissible for \(27\), so the least admissible multiple \(a(27)\) satisfies \(a(27)\leq999<1000\). It is positive, it is divisible by \(27\), and its reversal is divisible by \(27\). By the rigidity result modulo \(27\), it must be \(999\). Therefore
\[
a(27)=999.
\]
Also,
\[
10^{3^{3-2}}-1=10^3-1=999,
\]
so the equality holds for \(n=3\).

Finally,
\[
999999999=12345679\cdot81,
\]
and this number is again a palindrome. It is therefore admissible for \(81\), and the least admissible multiple satisfies
\[
a(81)\leq999999999<10^9.
\]
It is positive and both it and its reversal are divisible by \(81\). The rigidity result modulo \(81\) now gives
\[
a(81)=999999999.
\]
Since
\[
10^{3^{4-2}}-1=10^9-1=999999999,
\]
the equality holds for \(n=4\).

### 3. Short palindromic multiples for every higher power of \(3\)

We next construct, for every integer \(p\geq0\), a positive decimal palindrome \(V_p\) such that
\[
3^{5+p}\mid V_p
\]
and \(V_p\) has exactly
\[
L_p=11\cdot3^p
\]
decimal digits.

For the initial value take
\[
V_0=29799999792.
\]
Its decimal digit string is
\[
29799999792,
\]
which reads the same from right to left, so it is a palindrome. It has exactly eleven digits. Moreover,
\[
29799999792=243\cdot122633744=3^5\cdot122633744.
\]
Thus \(V_0\) has all the required properties.

Now suppose that \(V_p\) has been constructed, and let \(L=L_p\) be its number of decimal digits. Define
\[
V_{p+1}=V_p+10^L V_p+10^{2L}V_p
=V_p\bigl(1+10^L+10^{2L}\bigr).
\]
In decimal notation this is simply the concatenation of three copies of the \(L\)-digit string representing \(V_p\). Since that string is palindromic, the concatenation of three identical copies is also palindromic.

The concatenated number has exactly \(3L\) digits. Indeed, because \(V_p\) has exactly \(L\) digits,
\[
10^{L-1}\leq V_p<10^L.
\]
The highest shifted copy, \(10^{2L}V_p\), ensures that \(V_{p+1}\geq10^{3L-1}\), while the three blocks are each at most \(10^L-1\), so
\[
V_{p+1}\leq(10^L-1)(1+10^L+10^{2L})=10^{3L}-1<10^{3L}.
\]
Thus the length is exactly \(3L\), which equals
\[
3(11\cdot3^p)=11\cdot3^{p+1}.
\]

It remains to check divisibility. Modulo \(3\), one has \(10\equiv1\), so
\[
1+10^L+10^{2L}\equiv1+1+1\equiv0\pmod3.
\]
Therefore this factor is divisible by \(3\). Since the induction hypothesis gives \(3^{5+p}\mid V_p\), we obtain
\[
3^{6+p}=3^{5+(p+1)}\mid V_p(1+10^L+10^{2L})=V_{p+1}.
\]
This completes the induction.

Hence, for every \(p\geq0\), there exists a positive palindromic multiple \(V_p\) of \(3^{5+p}\) with exactly \(11\cdot3^p\) digits.

Because \(V_p\) is a palindrome,
\[
\operatorname{rev}(V_p)=V_p,
\]
and because \(3^{5+p}\mid V_p\), both \(V_p\) and its reversal are divisible by \(3^{5+p}\). Thus it is an admissible number in the definition of \(a(3^{5+p})\). Consequently,
\[
a(3^{5+p})\leq V_p<10^{11\cdot3^p}.
\]

On the other hand, when \(n=5+p\), the exponent appearing in the conjectured all-nines value is
\[
3^{n-2}=3^{3+p}=27\cdot3^p.
\]
Since \(11<27\),
\[
11\cdot3^p<27\cdot3^p=3^{3+p}.
\]
As the function \(r\mapsto10^r\) is strictly increasing,
\[
10^{11\cdot3^p}<10^{3^{3+p}}.
\]
Combining these inequalities gives
\[
a(3^{5+p})<10^{11\cdot3^p}<10^{3^{3+p}}.
\]
Since these are integers, the second strict inequality implies
\[
10^{11\cdot3^p}\leq10^{3^{3+p}}-1.
\]
Therefore
\[
a(3^{5+p})<10^{3^{3+p}}-1
=10^{3^{(5+p)-2}}-1.
\]
In particular,
\[
a(3^{5+p})\neq10^{3^{(5+p)-2}}-1
\]
for every \(p\geq0\), that is, for every \(n\geq5\).

### 4. Conclusion

Every integer \(n\geq2\) lies in exactly one of the cases
\[
n=2,\qquad n=3,\qquad n=4,\qquad n\geq5.
\]
For the first three cases we proved respectively
\[
a(3^2)=9=10^{3^0}-1,
\]
\[
a(3^3)=999=10^{3^1}-1,
\]
and
\[
a(3^4)=999999999=10^{3^2}-1.
\]
For every \(n\geq5\), the recursively constructed palindrome gives an admissible multiple strictly smaller than \(10^{3^{n-2}}-1\), so equality is impossible. Hence
\[
a(3^n)=10^{3^{n-2}}-1
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
n=2\text{ or }n=3\text{ or }n=4,
\]
as required.
